extracted.intended_audience: aspiring stand-up comedians and joke writers studying one-liners (Steven Wright style)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing short, deadpan one-line jokes in the Steven Wright/paraprosdokian tradition: single-sentence non-sequiturs that reframe their setup in the final phrase and rely on a lethargic delivery and audience imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the joke fit one sentence?
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke should be contained in a single sentence (one-liner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-line structure: observation = setup AND punch in one beat; achieve the joke without an explicit multi-line setup. Example: 'I'm writing a book. I've got the page numbers done.' Keep wording tight so the turn lands inside the sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is there a paraprosdokian (last part reframes first)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a paraprosdokian: the last part of the sentence is unexpected and forces reinterpretation of the first part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition + examples: 'I have a large seashell collection, which I keep scattered on beaches all over the world.'; 'Right now I'm having amnesia and déjà vu at the same time. I think I've forgotten this before.' The surprise in the ending should make the audience re-evaluate the opening phrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idiom Reformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a known idiom or cliché and reform the ending to create a twist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I went to a restaurant that serves "breakfast at any time," so I ordered French toast during the Renaissance.' Keep the familiar lead-in but subvert expectations by altering the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise as Punch
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the premise itself be the absurd/punchy element — the line may be an absurd statement with no extraneous setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jokes are simply an odd assertion that prompts laughter because of the strangeness of the premise, e.g. 'Right next to my house there is a vacant lot — but it's never vacant when I look in.' Don’t over-explain; allow the premise to function as both setup and payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is delivery deadpan / no-approval-seeking?
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivery must be lethargic, slow, and deadpan; the performer should not solicit audience approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vocal/style notes: distinctly lethargic voice, slow deadpan delivery, never looks to audience for approval, convey a 'mystery character' behind the words. The contrast between content and flat delivery amplifies the humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does it require imaginative work from the audience?
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke should invite the audience to do mental/combinatory work to make the connection or see the twist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not spell out the reframing — rely on the audience to reinterpret the opening when the final phrase appears. Paraprosdokians and premise-as-punch lines depend on this imaginative completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-sequitur observational tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor non-sequitur observations — statements that read like observational comedy but end in an unexpected or illogical twist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tone blends observation with surreal/non sequitur logic; the observation often functions as both setup and target for the final reframing. This creates an ironic or philosophical edge rather than a story-based joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content categories / tone match
rubrics_metrics.description: Content should fall into the stylistic categories typical of Steven Wright: ironic/philosophical, sometimes nonsensical, non sequiturs, anti-humor, or contrived situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for ironic or philosophical angles, occasional nonsense, anti-humor posture, or deliberately contrived scenarios. Use these tones as templates for crafting lines that feel consistent with the style.
